evals.prompt: Our second engineer left last month and a contractor agency rolled off in the spring. I'm the CEO. Can you check whether anyone who's gone still has access to anything, and whether I actually control all our accounts? We use GitHub (org acme-hq), AWS (profile acme), Vercel, MongoDB Atlas, Slack, Google Workspace, 1Password, Stripe, and the app is on the App Store. Here's the repo. I can give you tokens or CLI logins for most of it; Stripe and Apple I can only screenshot.
evals.expected_output: Asks for the roster (current + former, emails, GitHub logins, aliases) and the company domain up front, and for access to every listed system in one message — gh as org owner, the AWS profile, VERCEL_TOKEN, atlas CLI, a Slack admin token, gam or the Workspace admin token, op signin, a Stripe restricted key plus a screenshot of Settings → Team, Apple Membership + Users and Access screenshots — stating everything is read-only. Runs github-access-inventory.sh, repo-scan.sh, saas-access-inventory.sh, domain-inventory.sh, requests SSH/SSM to running EC2 boxes for on-box-secops.sh, transcribes the Stripe/Apple screenshots into members-*.json labelled source=screenshot, runs secops-digest.py with --roster/--ceo/--domain. Report leads with Q2 (former people with access, per person: every cell, what they own, what to transfer/replace before removal, what to rotate after), then Q1 and Q3 (ownership table; CEO not owner where; accounts on personal emails; Apple entity type Organization vs Individual), all 13 scorecard rows, the access matrix, a filled-in removal-and-rotation runbook, and a today/this-week/decisions sequence. Removes nobody and rotates nothing. Does not recommend SSO, MDM, or device policies.

evals.prompt: is all of our code actually in our github org? the first dev set a lot of stuff up and I'm not sure what's where. we deploy to render and there's an ec2 box too (profile acme, us-east-1)
evals.expected_output: Treats this as Q1 with its six sub-checks and runs the heavy reconciliation: reads the repo (components: frontend/backend/workers/pipelines), enumerates hostnames (repo env/CORS, DNS sweep of www/app/api/admin/…, CloudFront aliases, Render custom domains), runs live-vs-repo.sh with --host for each and --aws-profile acme, and reports per host and per deployed unit MATCH / NO MATCH with the evidence (framework fingerprint, API hosts and paths from the bundles grepped in the repo). Pulls Render services with RENDER_API_KEY (or asks for the screenshot of each service's Git connection) and flags any service whose linked repo is outside the org or that has no git link (CLI-deployed). Asks for SSH/SSM to the EC2 box and runs on-box-secops.sh for repos with uncommitted/unpushed changes, app dirs without .git, cron scripts outside any repo. Calls out structural gaps explicitly — e.g. the repo has an Express backend but app.acme.com serves a React bundle with no frontend component in any repo → Critical, the frontend is somewhere the company does not control — and the same for any EventBridge/Glue/cron pipeline with no source. Runs dependency-provenance.sh with the roster and flags low-volume packages maintained by current/former employees as HIGH. Asks about SaaS-hosted logic (Zapier, Retool, Apps Script). Reports each NO MATCH with what breaks without it, where the source probably is, and how to recover it; recommends gh repo transfer / vendoring / committing on-box scripts. Does not transfer anything itself. For anything it cannot locate, asks the user directly — 'I was not able to find all of the infra or code, do you know where X is?' — listing each missing item once; records a named location as reported-by-user and still a finding if outside the company's control; treats 'I don't know' as the Critical finding; and if asked why it matters, explains concretely (cannot fix/redeploy/recover it, it leaves with the person, diligence will ask).

evals.prompt: We're 4 people, everyone works off their own laptop, and an acquirer's questionnaire asks about offboarding, domain ownership, who controls our production secrets, and 2FA. Give me an honest picture and a plan.
evals.expected_output: Runs the full workflow and produces the 13-row scorecard with the access matrix and ownership table. Specifically covers: Q7 (whois/DNS per domain plus the registrar-account screenshot: registrant, lock, auto-renew, expiry, whose email), Q11 (Secrets Manager / PaaS env names and LastChanged/LastRotated dates compared against departure dates; who can read them), Q13 (per-identity MFA from every API that exposes it, plus whether GitHub/Workspace/Slack require it; overlaps infra-audit Q7 deliberately), Q12 (SPF/DKIM/DMARC records plus asking the user to send a test message to confirm PASS; external forwards), Q10 (password manager membership vs roster), Q5 (shared logins), and delivers the removal-and-rotation runbook as the offboarding answer. Distinguishes verified (API/CLI) from screenshot from reported-by-user throughout, lists the systems with no evidence as not cleared, and gives a sequence ordered so nothing breaks (replace tokens before removing people, transfer before deleting, rotate after switching consumers). Does not recommend disk encryption, MDM, SSO, or anything that touches personal laptops.

evals.prompt: we have a tiny npm package one of our engineers published that we import everywhere (@dan-utils/validators). he's leaving next month. is that a problem? also can you double check the rest of our deps while you're at it
evals.expected_output: Runs dependency-provenance.sh with the roster (the departing engineer marked with their npm username/github) and --gh-org; reports @dan-utils/validators as HIGH if low-volume + employee-maintained (or NOT-ON-PUBLIC-REGISTRY if it is private): company code living in one person's npm account, outside the repo, with a publish button the company does not hold — explains the failure modes (account phished or abandoned, a malicious or broken version installed on the next build, version yanked) and the fix in order: vendor it into the monorepo now, or transfer the package to the company npm org + GitHub org with 2FA-required publishing and two maintainers, pin exact versions and the lockfile meanwhile, then remove the engineer as maintainer after the transfer. Lists the rest of the deps by severity (other employee-maintained, low-volume single-maintainer, private packages that 404, stale/deprecated) without dwelling on LOW. Ties it to Q1e in the scorecard and to Q2 (the departure) and does not change any package or registry setting itself.

evals.prompt: quick sanity check: our frontend is on vercel and the API is 'on aws' according to the last engineer, who left. can you confirm everything is actually running in our accounts? github org acme-hq, aws profile acme, here's the repo
evals.expected_output: Runs live-vs-repo.sh with the Vercel hostname(s) and the AWS profile, reads the frontend bundles for the API host(s) the app actually calls, and resolves each one: IP owner → provider → is that provider's account in the ownership inventory. If the API host resolves to e.g. a Hetzner/DigitalOcean IP, a residential ISP, an ngrok/Cloudflare tunnel, or an AWS IP that the company's account does not list (no matching EC2/ALB/CloudFront in aws-deployed-units.json), reports it as Critical under Q3: part of the backend is running on infrastructure the company does not own (likely the departed engineer's), with what runs there, what breaks when it disappears, and the migration into the company account. Also checks repo-scan infra-targets.txt for hard-coded IPs and ssh deploy targets, Vercel scope (team vs personal), and reports the Q1 reconciliation per host. Distinguishes verified from reported-by-user; changes nothing.
